taxi.fareNote: Fares are usually negotiated or fixed before the ride rather than metered; app-based rides (Uber) are cheaper and more transparent.

emergency.note: 911 is the unified national emergency line for police, fire and ambulance; Cruz Roja Salvadoreña also runs ambulance services.

avoid.reason: Crime dropped sharply since 2022 — now among the safest capitals; stay in San Benito/Escalón/Santa Elena; minor petty crime in the historic downtown

hood_desc: Upscale dining, nightlife and business hub anchored by the World Trade Center; popular with business travelers and those wanting easy access to good restaurants and bars.
Leafy, affluent residential district lined with embassies, boutiques and cafés; a safe, walkable base for travelers who want a quieter upscale feel.
The historic downtown core with the National Palace, Metropolitan Cathedral and Plaza Barrios; atmospheric but rougher-edged, best for budget travelers sticking to daytime sightseeing.
Bustling commercial strip anchored by the landmark Metrocentro mall, with cinemas, food courts and mid-range hotels; convenient and central for first-time visitors.
Modern, low-rise business district south of the city near Multiplaza mall and La Gran Vía lifestyle center; widely considered the safest, most polished area, favored by corporate travelers.

water.note: Avoid tap water; drink bottled or purified water.

sys.n: SITRAMSS (Sistema Integrado de Transporte del Área Metropolitana de San Salvador)

transit.pay: Most city buses and microbuses are cash pay-as-you-board (small coins/bills handed to the driver or fare collector). The SITRAMSS BRT corridor uses a rechargeable prepaid smart card tapped at station turnstiles. There is no single unified fare card covering all routes.
transit.hours: Most buses run roughly 5am-8pm with sparse coverage after dark; taxis and rideshare apps are the standard option at night.
transit.note: Bus routes are not always clearly signed for visitors and can be crowded; many travelers rely on taxis or Uber instead, especially at night.

tip.r: Many restaurants add a 10% service charge to the bill; if not included, tipping ~10% is customary. Rounding up for taxis and casual service is appreciated but not required.

landmarks: Metropolitan Cathedral of San Salvador
This bold, colorfully tiled cathedral dominates the historic center and holds the crypt of Archbishop Óscar Romero, making it a powerful spiritual and architectural landmark.
National Palace (Palacio Nacional)
A gleaming neoclassical palace of white marble and Italian tilework, this former seat of government now welcomes visitors to admire its ornate halls and courtyards.
Monumento al Divino Salvador del Mundo
El Salvador's most iconic emblem, this hilltop monument depicts Christ atop a globe and volcano, symbolizing national identity and offering sweeping city views.
Iglesia El Rosario
Behind a plain concrete exterior lies a breathtaking curved interior awash in stained-glass light, making this modernist church one of the city's most photographed surprises.
Teatro Nacional de San Salvador
Central America's oldest national theater, built in French Renaissance style in the early 1900s, dazzles with gilded interiors and remains a hub for the arts.
Plaza Gerardo Barrios
The historic heart of the capital, this shaded plaza centers on an equestrian statue of a former president, flanked by the cathedral and national palace.
Museo Nacional de Antropología (MUNA)
El Salvador's leading anthropology museum showcases pre-Columbian artifacts and Maya heritage through immersive exhibits inside a striking modern building.
Puerta del Diablo
Two massive volcanic rock formations frame a dramatic mountain gap on the city's outskirts, rewarding hikers with panoramic valley views and legendary local folklore.
Parque Cuscatlán
A vast urban park featuring a moving civil war memorial engraved with victims' names, alongside gardens, murals, and exhibition halls beloved by locals.
Museo de Arte de El Salvador (MARTE)
The country's leading visual-arts museum, set beside Parque Cuscatlán in San Benito, tracing two centuries of Salvadoran painting alongside rotating exhibitions.

train.note: El Salvador has no regular passenger rail. The state operator FENADESAL runs only occasional short heritage/commuter excursions, so travel between cities is by bus.

intl.to: Guatemala City, Tegucigalpa & San Pedro Sula (Honduras), Managua (Nicaragua), San José (Costa Rica) & Panama City

bus.note: King Quality / Puerto Bus and Pullmantur also run comfortable coaches to Guatemala City and Honduras from their own terminals in San Salvador. Bring your passport for the CA-4 border crossings.

ferry.note: No international passenger ferries from El Salvador. Small boats cross the Gulf of Fonseca informally, but there is no scheduled service; travellers use buses instead.

half.name: El Boquerón National Park
half.blurb: The country's most accessible volcano, with easy trails to a vast dormant summit crater.

half.name: Suchitoto
half.blurb: A cobblestoned colonial town on a hillside overlooking the shimmering Lake Suchitlán.

half.name: Ruta de las Flores
half.blurb: A scenic mountain route linking colorful coffee towns known for murals, food, and flowers.

half.name: Santa Ana Volcano
half.blurb: El Salvador's highest volcano, rewarding hikers with a turquoise crater lake at its summit.

half.name: Playa El Tunco
half.blurb: A laid-back black-sand beach town celebrated for its surf breaks and sunset scene.

half.name: Joya de Cerén
half.blurb: A UNESCO-listed Maya farming village preserved by ash, the Pompeii of the Americas.
